extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, media researchers, journalism students, and newsroom editors interested in news selection theory
extracted.subtask_description: A theoretical framework for understanding and evaluating how individual journalists and news organizations select stories, emphasizing cognitive/psychological drivers behind newsworthiness and observable newsroom behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for Social Validation of Perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists seek confirmation that their perceptions of events are shared by others to reduce uncertainty about reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validation is achieved by checking what other journalists are covering (pack journalism), citing authoritative sources whose definition becomes 'the' definition, and following established beats and topics where consensus exists. This need explains why presence of coverage elsewhere increases a story's newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to Preserve Existing Predispositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists prefer information consistent with their pre-existing beliefs and avoid information that would require updating priors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears as confirmation bias in story pursuit, source preferences favoring those who confirm worldviews, and frame inheritance that perpetuates initial interpretations; leads to selecting stories that fit rather than challenge priors.

rubrics_metrics.name: News Factors (Object Properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Event- or object-level structural news values (the Galtung–Ruge style features) that make an occurrence notable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as one source of influence on selection—properties of events themselves (e.g., magnitude, timeliness, proximity) remain relevant but are processed through psychological mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional Objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: The outlet's commercial, political, or public-service mission shapes what is pursued and published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different institutional goals (profit, partisan alignment, public service) bias selection toward stories that serve those objectives; editors' expressed norms may conflict with these objectives but behavior is influenced nonetheless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulative Power of PR Sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategic communicators and PR professionals can pre-package newsworthy material to influence newsroom selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-packaged framing and accessible authoritative sources reduce reporter uncertainty and increase the likelihood of coverage; PR activity functions as an external driver of what gets selected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective Beliefs of Journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual reporters' personal political attitudes, ideological priors, and professional norms influence story selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These subjective beliefs interact with other influences: they bias attention, source choice, and framing; they are a distinct source of variance separate from institutional or event properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underlying Psychological Processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The cognitive mechanisms—validation-seeking and predisposition-preserving cognition—that shape how journalists process other influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donsbach's principal contribution: rather than just listing news-values, explain why those values operate via two universal psychological needs; this lens reinterprets other influences (news factors, institutions, PR, subjective beliefs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pack Convergence (Pack Journalism) as a News Value
rubrics_metrics.description: A story being covered by other outlets functions as a news value because it validates a reporter's perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage by peers reduces uncertainty and thus increases the perceived legitimacy and reportability of a story; this produces herd-like convergence across outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with named, institutionally-backed or authoritative sources are favored because they reduce reporter uncertainty about facts and definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority serves the reporter's need for validation and mirrors objectivity rituals (e.g., citing institutional sources) at a cognitive level; presence of authoritative sources increases story selectability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predisposition Compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that confirm rather than challenge journalists' worldviews are more likely to be pursued and published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compatibility with priors makes stories easier to compose and less cognitively costly; results in selective attention and reporting that perpetuates existing frames and beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame Familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that fit recognized narrative templates or familiar frames feel more 'real' and are more readily reportable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame inheritance—using existing frames to interpret events—reduces uncertainty and effort; unfamiliar frames are less likely to be adopted, even if they might be more accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter Self-Image Compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that match a reporter's professional identity (investigative, beat, soft-news, etc.) are pursued more readily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A story that aligns with how a reporter sees their role supports motivation and professional validation, increasing selection probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive Foundation for News Values
rubrics_metrics.description: News-values operate because they map onto general psychological needs (validation and preserving predispositions), providing an explanatory foundation for observed selection patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion reframes traditional news-values as manifestations of cognitive needs, suggesting that measures of newsworthiness should account for psychological drivers, not only structural event features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction of Pack Journalism / Herd Behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: The model predicts that outlets will converge on the same stories not only for competition but because coverage by others validates reporters' reality judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains cross-outlet convergence as partly cognitive-validation-driven rather than purely institutional or market-driven; relevant when modeling homepage story overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction of Confirmation Bias in Source Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists tend to return to sources that confirm priors and avoid those that challenge them, producing structural bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source selection patterns should be evaluated for bias: frequent use of confirming sources is an indicator of predisposition-preserving cognition at work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalizability via Cross-Outlet Correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: Story selection can be operationalized and tested as partly driven by what other outlets are covering—measurable through cross-outlet (e.g., homepage) correlation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an empirical strategy: model story choice including variables for other outlets' coverage; useful for homepage/newsroom dataset analysis to detect validation-driven selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation for Norm–Behavior Gap
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors may verbally reject metric- or pack-driven selection because it conflicts with professional self-image, but behavior is nevertheless shaped by the same psychological needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating newsroom practices, account for discrepancies between stated norms and observable choices: reported editorial principles may not align with selection behavior due to underlying cognitive motives.
